title: Purification in Islam
description: What spiritual and physical purification mean in Islam, the steps of wudu and ghusl, and answers to common questions about ritual cleanliness.

sections.heading: What purification means in Islam
sections.content:
Purification (taharah) sits high on the list in Islam. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said, **"Cleanliness is half of faith"** (Sahih Muslim 223). Purification runs past hygiene and into your spiritual life.

It works on two levels. The first is **spiritual purification**, meaning clearing envy, arrogance, and dishonesty out of your heart. That work never really finishes. The second is **physical purification**, the ritual washing that gets you ready for acts of worship like prayer and touching the Quran.

Physical purification is one of the first practical things a new Muslim learns. It looks like a lot of detail written down, and it is simple once you have done it three or four times. Wudu (ablution) is a pause built into the day: two minutes to wash off distraction before you stand in front of Allah.

Islam's concern with cleanliness goes past the ritual too. Keeping your body, your clothes, and your prayer space clean is part of the faith. Many Muslims find these habits give the rest of the day a shape it did not have before.

sections.heading: Wudu: the washing before prayer
sections.content:
Wudu is the ritual washing you do before prayer. You need it whenever you are in a state of minor impurity, which covers using the restroom, passing gas, sleeping deeply, and the like. The steps:

1. **Begin with the intention (niyyah):** in your heart, intend to perform wudu for the sake of Allah. Nothing needs to be said aloud.
2. **Say "Bismillah"** (In the name of Allah).
3. **Wash your hands** three times, making sure water gets between the fingers.
4. **Rinse your mouth** three times, swirling water around and spitting it out.
5. **Rinse your nose** three times, sniffing water gently into the nostrils and blowing it out.
6. **Wash your face** three times, from the hairline to the chin and from ear to ear.
7. **Wash your right arm** from fingertips to elbow three times, then your **left arm** the same way.
8. **Wipe your head** once: wet your hands and pass them from the front of your head to the back, then forward again.
9. **Wipe your ears** once, with your index fingers inside and your thumbs behind.
10. **Wash your right foot** up to the ankle three times, then your **left foot** the same way.

Washing each part once is the minimum, and three times is the Sunnah. That is the whole thing, and it takes a couple of minutes. After wudu you are in a state of ritual purity and ready to pray.

**What breaks wudu?** Using the restroom, passing gas, deep sleep and losing consciousness. A hadith says prayer is not accepted from someone whose wudu has broken until they make wudu again (Sahih al-Bukhari 135). Bleeding, vomiting and touching the private parts are treated differently by the schools, and the washing tool sets out the views.

Your wudu stays valid until something breaks it. If you made wudu for Dhuhr and nothing broke it, you can pray Asr on the same wudu.

sections.heading: Ghusl: the full body wash
sections.content:
Ghusl is a full-body ritual wash, required after certain things put you in a state of major impurity. The usual ones are:

- After sexual intercourse
- After a wet dream (for both men and women)
- After menstruation ends (for women)
- After postpartum bleeding ends (for women)
- When someone becomes Muslim (required in some views and recommended in others; a hadith reports the Prophet telling a new Muslim to bathe, Sunan Abi Dawud 355)

The steps of ghusl:

1. **Make your intention** in your heart to perform ghusl.
2. **Say "Bismillah."**
3. **Wash your hands** three times.
4. **Wash your private areas** to remove any impurity.
5. **Perform a complete wudu** as described above.
6. **Pour water over your head** three times, making sure it reaches the roots of your hair.
7. **Wash the right side of your body,** then the **left side,** so that water reaches every part of your skin.

The principle is simple: water must reach every part of your body, and that alone is the minimum. You can do it wherever you normally wash, with the intention set and a bit of care that nothing gets missed.

After ghusl you are in a state of complete purity and do not need a separate wudu for prayer, because the ghusl already covers it. If something breaks your wudu afterward, like using the restroom, you only need to repeat the wudu, not the ghusl.

sections.heading: Tayammum: dry purification
sections.content:
Islam is practical, and Allah does not load anyone past what they can carry. Sometimes water is not available, and sometimes using it would hurt you: traveling somewhere with no water, being ill in a way that water would make worse, or having a wound that has to stay dry.

For those cases there is **tayammum** (dry purification). How it works:

1. **Make your intention** to perform tayammum.
2. **Strike your palms** lightly on clean earth, sand, stone, or any natural surface with dust on it.
3. **Wipe your face** once with your palms.
4. **Strike the surface again** and **wipe your right arm** to the elbow with your left hand, then your **left arm** with your right hand.

This is the Hanafi method. Another method uses a single strike and wipes the face and the hands to the wrists (Sahih al-Bukhari 338). The Quran allows tayammum for people who are ill, travelling or cannot find water (4:43 and 5:6).

Tayammum stands in for both wudu and ghusl while water is out of reach. Once you can get to water and use it, you go back to the usual wudu or ghusl.

Tayammum is a clear example of how Islam builds in ease. The Quran states: **"Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship"** (2:185). What you owe is your best with what you actually have.

sections.heading: Clean clothes and a clean place (najasah)
sections.content:
The Quran says, **"Purify your garments"** (74:4). Your body, your clothes and the spot where you pray should be free of impurity (najasah). The rules are simpler than most people fear. When a man urinated in the Prophet's masjid, the Prophet (peace be upon him) told his companions to pour a bucket of water over it and said, **"You have been sent to make things easy"** (Sahih al-Bukhari 220).

**What counts as impure.** Urine, stool and blood are the ones you will meet most. The Shafi'i answer we link sorts impurity into three kinds: heavy (a dog or a pig), light (the urine of a baby boy under two who only drinks milk) and moderate (everything else). The schools differ on some things, such as a dog's saliva and alcohol, so ask your teacher about the ones that come up in your home.

**How to clean it.** For most impurity, wash the spot until the substance, its colour and its smell are gone as far as you reasonably can. A floor is cleaned by pouring water over it (Sahih al-Bukhari 220). Menstrual blood on clothes is rubbed, washed and rinsed, and the garment can then be worn for prayer (Sahih al-Bukhari 227).

**A baby's urine.** The Prophet poured water over the urine of a milk-fed baby boy on his clothes and did not wash it further (Sahih al-Bukhari 223). The Shafi'i answer we link calls this sprinkling. In other cases, or when you are unsure, wash it normally.

**Dogs.** A vessel a dog has licked is washed seven times (Sahih Muslim 279a). In the Shafi'i school a dog counts as a heavy impurity, washed seven times with one of the washes using earth. The schools differ on whether a dog itself is impure. For prayer, what matters is your body, your clothes and the spot you pray on, so a clean corner of the house is enough.

**Alcohol in perfume, deodorant and hand sanitiser.** The Hanafi answer we link says alcohol that is not made from wine is not ritually impure and can be used on the body. The same answer says avoiding it is more cautious, because some scholars, including some Hanafis, were stricter. Ask your teacher what your school says.

**Laundry.** A Hanafi answer says clothes that come out of the washing machine with no trace of filth can be taken as clean. It suggests rinsing a soiled spot before the wash. There is no need to rewash loads that a family member has already done.

**Small amounts.** The Shafi'i answer we link excuses filth too small to see with ordinary eyes, your own blood or pus whether there is a lot or a little, and a small amount of someone else's blood. The other schools set their own limits, so ask your teacher.

**A mark you notice after praying.** A Hanafi answer deals with a small mark found in underwear after the prayer that was not there at wudu. It says you do not repeat the prayer, because the mark is taken to have happened at the latest possible time. For other situations, ask.

**A doubt is not impurity.** The Prophet told someone who thought he had passed wind in prayer not to leave it unless he heard a sound or noticed a smell (Sahih al-Bukhari 137). Scholars apply the same idea more widely: something you know to be clean stays clean until you are sure it is not. That is a general rule drawn from this hadith, not its exact subject.

A few habits help:

- Keep one set of clothes you know are clean for praying at work.
- Rinse a spot before it dries, then wash the item as normal.
- If a pet or a baby is part of home life, keep a small spray bottle of water near your prayer spot.
- If you are unsure whether your clothes are clean, go with what you know for certain and ask a teacher afterwards. Do not skip the prayer over it.

sections.heading: Common questions about purification
sections.content:
**"Do I need wudu to read the Quran?"**
Scholars generally agree you need wudu to physically touch the Arabic text of the Quran (the mushaf). You can recite from memory, read a translation, or listen without wudu. Many new Muslims read from Quran apps on their phones, and most scholars allow this without wudu, since you are not touching the text itself.

**"What if I have a medical condition that makes wudu difficult?"**
Islam makes room for medical needs. If you have a wound that should not get wet, you can wipe over a bandage instead. If you have a condition that keeps breaking your wudu, incontinence for example, the Hanafi school counts you as an excused person when the condition leaves no time for wudu and a prayer. You make wudu once the prayer time begins and pray even while the condition continues, and that wudu lasts until the time ends (the SeekersGuidance answer we link). The other schools set this out differently, and the washing tool has more. For your own situation, ask a knowledgeable community member or a scholar.

**"Can I wipe over my socks instead of washing my feet?"**
Yes, under certain conditions. If you put your socks on while in a state of wudu, you can wipe over them, passing wet hands over the top, instead of taking them off and washing your feet. The concession lasts 24 hours for residents and 72 hours for travelers. The schools differ on which socks count: the Hanafi school asks for socks sturdy enough to walk in that water does not soak through, while other teaching allows ordinary socks. Ask your imam which view your community follows.

**"I have trouble remembering all the steps. Is that okay?"**
Of course. Wudu is a skill like any other and it takes repetition. Many new Muslims tape a small reference card near the sink at first, or watch a video a few times. Inside a few weeks it becomes automatic. Do your best, and know that Allah takes the effort and the sincerity.

**"Does nail polish affect wudu?"**
Regular nail polish forms a barrier that keeps water off the nail, which leaves the wudu incomplete. Take the polish off before wudu. If you made wudu before putting it on, you can pray with that wudu. This is practical information rather than a judgment on anyone.

**"How do I clean myself after using the toilet?"**
Wipe with toilet paper, then wash with water if you can, using your left hand. The Hanafi answer we link says paper then water is best, and paper alone meets the basic sunnah as long as the mess has not spread beyond the exit. If it has spread further, washing with water is required. The washing tool has the full steps, including what to do in a washroom with no bidet.
